Every excerpt is preceded by a provenance marker of the form `<!-- source: <id> -->`.

Your only job is to list the film samples the paper reports results for. Do NOT report any measured values; later questions ask for those.

{

    {"sample_id": "<short stable id>", "label": "<human readable description>",

     "source_ids": ["<id>", ...]},
    ...
  ],
  "no_tco_film": <true|false>
}

Rules:
1. Create one entry per distinct film sample / deposition condition set that the paper reports results for (e.g. one per O2 flow rate, per power, per substrate temperature).
   A sample is a TCO or transparent-electrode film that this paper deposits itself. The other layers of a device -- a perovskite or organic absorber / active layer, charge-transport layers, thin buffer layers (e.g. evaporated MoOx, WOx, NbOy, VOx, or nanoparticle SnO2 / ZnO under an electrode), metal contacts -- are never samples, nor is a whole device, nor a purchased substrate (commercial ITO or FTO glass). When the paper varies only those other layers, the TCO film it deposits is still a single sample. A multilayer transparent electrode (oxide/metal/oxide such as ITO/Ag/ITO or WO3/Ag/WO3) is one film: its thin metal interlayer is part of it, not a metal contact. Changes to the TCO film itself do make separate samples: each deposition condition, each thickness of any of its layers, and each post-treatment (as-deposited, annealed at 150 °C, annealed at 230 °C...) is its own sample. So is each substrate the paper compares the film's properties on (glass vs. a metal foil); the same film merely deposited on a second substrate to characterise it (Si for XRD, a TEM grid) is the same sample.

5. Only report samples the paper actually reports results for. Never guess and never invent a series: if the paper studies a single film, return exactly one sample; if the excerpts name none, return an empty list.

Typically, three substrates of fused silica $( 3 0 \times 3 0 \times$ 3 mm), Corning glass (same size), and silicon $( 1 0 ~ \times ~ 1 0 ~ \times$ 1 mm) were simultaneously mounted onto the sample holder for the depositions. The centrally positioned oxygen inlets over the magnetrons ensure a homogeneous oxygen distribution in the plasma. Following a preoptimization with respect to oxygen flow rate and magnetrons’ powers, a systematic series of $\mathrm { S n O } _ { x } \mathrm { : T a }$ thin films was grown as a function of the oxygen flow rate at a deposition temperature of $2 2 5 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ with a working pressure of 1.1 Pa Ar. The formation of the transparent conductive oxide  $ SnO_{2} $:Ta by reactive direct-current magnetron sputtering at a low temperature of  $ 225^{\circ}C $ was studied as a function of the oxygen flow rate using a pilot-scale setup. Beginning with a mixture of  $ \beta $-Sn and SnO as majority phases and minority fractions of  $ Sn_{3}O_{4} $ and  $ SnO_{2} $ at very low  $ O_{2} $ flows, up to the formation of phase-pure rutile-type  $ SnO_{2} $:Ta at higher flow rates, a systematic evolution of the phase structure is observed. The  $ SnO_{2} $:Ta (0.70 at.% Ta) film grown at optimized flow conditions exhibits a transmittance of >80% from 500 to 2500 nm and a specific resistivity of  $ 0.3\ \Omega cm $. While the transmittance is competitive, the resistivity is in the upper range of that reported for low-temperature-deposited  $ SnO_{2} $:Ta films in research lab studies. Based on X-ray diffraction, Raman spectroscopy, optical spectroscopy, and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy, we conclude that the small crystallite size, microstrain, and point defects caused by the low growth temperature might prevent charge carrier activation, even though the Ta dopant is incorporated as  $ Ta^{5+} $ in the rutile-type  $ SnO_{2} $ lattice.

Among the three classical transparent conductive oxides (TCOs) such as  $ In_{2}O_{3} $, ZnO, and  $ SnO_{2} $, the latter is distinguished by a high chemical, mechanical, and thermal stability [1-3]. The most abundantly used dopant for  $ SnO_{2} $ is fluorine [4-7].  $ SnO_{2}:F $ can be used as a transparent electrode in display technologies, as a low-emissivity glass coating to improve the energy efficiency of buildings by reducing the infrared heat transmission while still retaining the transparency for visible light, or as a spectrally selective coating for solar collectors [3, 8, 9]. Recently, the research focus for  $ SnO_{2} $-based TCOs has shifted to the investigation of tantalum-doped  $ SnO_{2} $ (TTO) thin films because of their superior electrical properties and higher thermal stability in vacuum and air [10-14]. This latter material property is especially critical as these films can find an application as a capacitor electrode in data storage devices, or as a solar-selective transmitter in concentrated solar power plants that require a heat resistance up to 800°C [15, 16]. Because this material demonstrates the potential to be used in a wide range of applications, the necessary tunability to meet the different technical specifications requires the use of scalable low-temperature deposition techniques.

SnOₓ:Ta thin films were deposited by reactive DC–MS in a pilot-scale sputter chamber of the company Nano4Energy [23]. Typically, three substrates of fused silica (30 × 30 × 3 mm), Corning glass (same size), and silicon (10 × 10 × 1 mm) were simultaneously mounted onto the sample holder for the depositions.
